title: The history of the induction hob
tagline: 190 years from a ring of iron in London to a 2 kW hob on an Indian kitchen counter.
intro: Induction started as a laboratory surprise: change a magnetic field and a current appears in nearby metal. For decades it was used to brake discs and melt steel. It reached the kitchen only when glass that could take a hot pan and fast, cheap power switches came along, and in India it is now part of the push to cook with electricity.

eras.name: Changing fields, moving currents
eras.summary: Scientists find that a changing magnetic field drives currents in metal, that those currents push back, and that they make heat.

eras.name: Heating metal from the inside
eras.summary: Engineers put metal inside coils to melt and heat it with its own eddy currents. The first patents for cooking this way are filed.

eras.name: Into the kitchen
eras.summary: A tough glass-ceramic, a newspaper demonstration and the first induction ranges. Fast power switches make the electronics cheaper.

eras.name: A hob for every kitchen
eras.summary: Induction rice cookers, cheap single-zone hobs, safety and energy rules, and India's programmes for cooking with electricity.

events.title: A spinning disc drags a magnet
events.text: Arago found that a spinning copper disc makes a hanging magnet turn with it, though copper is not magnetic. Nobody could explain it yet.
events.why: It was the first sign of eddy currents, the effect that heats a pan on a hob.

events.title: Faraday's induction ring
events.text: Faraday wound two coils on one iron ring. When he switched a current on or off in one, a needle on the other coil kicked. A changing magnetic field had made a current.
events.why: Every induction hob is this ring with the pan as the second coil.

events.title: Induced currents push back
events.text: Lenz stated the rule for which way an induced current flows: always so as to oppose the change that made it.
events.why: It is why eddy currents brake moving metal and why they cost energy, which ends up as heat.

events.title: Currents that heat a disc
events.text: Foucault spun a copper disc between the poles of a magnet. It became much harder to turn, and the disc grew hot. The swirling currents inside it are still called Foucault currents in France.
events.why: Heat from eddy currents is exactly what an induction hob makes in the pan.

events.title: Heating metal with fast-changing fields
events.text: A German engineering chronology credits Colby with using high-frequency alternating fields to heat metals. Details of this early work are thin.
events.why: Higher frequency squeezes the current into a thinner skin and heats faster.

events.title: An induction furnace melts steel
events.text: Kjellin, a metallurgical chemist, built an induction furnace for steel. The metal itself formed the loop in which the current was induced, so it heated from within.
events.why: Induction heating became an industrial tool long before it became a cooker.

events.title: A patent for cooking by induction
events.text: Berry applied for one of the first patents for heating cooking vessels by induction. A German patent by Simon Hohlfeld followed in 1909.
events.why: The idea of cooking with eddy currents is more than a century old.

events.title: The high-frequency furnace
events.text: Northrup developed a high-frequency induction furnace that melts metal in a crucible inside a coil, for the Ajax companies. Sources date the work to about 1914 and his US patent to 1918.
events.why: Coreless, high-frequency coils are the direct ancestors of the flat coil under a hob.

events.title: A glass that will not crack
events.text: A faulty furnace overheated a sample of glass, which turned milky and bounced when dropped. Stookey had made the first glass-ceramic, sold as Pyroceram.
events.why: Hob tops are glass-ceramic because it barely expands when a hot pan sits on it.

events.title: Boiling water through a newspaper
events.text: Frigidaire's demonstration stove boiled a pot of water with a sheet of newspaper between the pot and the hob. The paper did not burn. The stove was never sold.
events.why: It showed the magic trick of induction: the pan heats, the surface does not.

events.title: The Cool Top
events.text: Westinghouse showed a single-zone Cool Top induction range at a home builders' convention. It drove its coil at about 25 kHz with transistors made for car ignitions.
events.why: It was one of the first induction cookers made to be sold to homes.

events.title: Cool Top 2 goes on sale
events.text: A few hundred Cool Top 2 ranges were made, with four zones of about 1,600 W at about 27 kHz under a Pyroceram top. They cost about $1,500 with a set of pans, and production stopped in 1975.
events.why: The idea worked, but the electronics were too costly for most homes.

events.title: The IGBT
events.text: India-born engineer B. Jayant Baliga conceived a switch that combines a MOS transistor's easy control with a bipolar transistor's high current: the insulated-gate bipolar transistor. He received the US National Medal of Technology and Innovation for it in 2011.
events.why: Cheap, fast IGBTs are the switches inside almost every induction hob.

events.title: Induction in a US department store
events.text: Sears sold a four-zone induction range in the mid-1980s.
events.why: Induction was slowly becoming a product you could buy off the shelf.

events.title: The induction rice cooker
events.text: Matsushita made the first induction-heating rice cooker. A coil heats the whole inner pot itself, instead of a hot plate warming only its bottom.
events.why: Induction found its first mass market in Japanese kitchens.

events.title: Hobs that heat aluminium
events.text: Panasonic developed an all-metal induction cooker that runs at much higher frequencies, said to be up to 120 kHz, so aluminium and copper pans heat too.
events.why: A thinner skin depth makes even good conductors heat, at the cost of harder electronics.

events.title: Exposure guidelines for low-frequency fields
events.text: The International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection published guidelines for fields from 1 Hz to 100 kHz. Germany's radiation protection office quotes its reference value of 27 µT for hobs.
events.why: It is the yardstick used to check the stray field of induction hobs.

events.title: A cap on subsidised LPG
events.text: India capped subsidised LPG cylinders at six a year per household, raised to nine in January 2013 and twelve in 2014. Reports at the time expected more homes to buy induction cookers.
events.why: The price of cooking gas has long shaped whether Indian families try an induction hob.

events.title: Ujjwala brings LPG to poorer homes
events.who: Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas
events.text: The Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana was launched to give LPG connections to poor households. By March 2024 it had released over 10 crore connections.
events.why: LPG is the stove most Indian induction hobs are compared with.

events.title: Induction stoves under the BIS mark
events.text: BIS recorded its first licence for an induction stove under IS 302-2-6, the safety standard for cooking ranges and hobs, as the product came under compulsory registration.
events.why: Hobs sold in India must meet a national safety standard.

events.title: Go Electric
events.text: India launched the Go Electric campaign to spread the word about electric vehicles and electric cooking, such as induction hobs and electric pressure cookers.
events.why: Cooking with electricity became official energy policy.

events.title: An award for induction
events.text: ENERGY STAR gave residential induction cooking tops its Emerging Technology Award, putting them at about 85% efficient against 75–80% for electric resistance and about 32% for gas.
events.why: These are the efficiency figures the power chapter starts with.

events.title: 20 lakh induction cooktops
events.text: EESL launched the National Efficient Cooking Programme, planning to distribute 20 lakh energy-efficient induction cooktops across India.
events.why: It is India's largest programme so far to put induction hobs into homes.

events.title: A star label for induction hobs
events.text: India notified a star label for countertop induction hobs under IS 19014:2022, with a minimum thermal efficiency of 80%. In April 2026 the compulsory start was moved to 1 January 2027.
events.why: Buyers will be able to compare hobs by how much energy they waste.

people.name: Michael Faraday
people.note: Discovered electromagnetic induction with a ring of iron and two coils.

people.name: Léon Foucault
people.note: Showed that eddy currents brake and heat a copper disc spinning near a magnet.

people.name: Fredrik Adolf Kjellin
people.note: Built an early induction furnace for melting steel at Gysinge.

people.name: Edwin Fitch Northrup
people.note: Developed the high-frequency coreless induction furnace.

people.name: S. Donald Stookey
people.note: Made the first glass-ceramic, the kind of material used for hob tops.

people.name: B. Jayant Baliga
people.note: Conceived the IGBT, the fast switch inside induction hobs.

facts: In the 1950s Frigidaire boiled water on an induction hob with a sheet of newspaper between the pot and the hob, and the paper did not burn.
In a cast-iron pan on a hob running at 24 kHz, almost all the heat is made in the bottom quarter of a millimetre.
Westinghouse's Cool Top 2 of 1973, one of the first induction ranges for homes, cost about $1,500 with its pans.
The switch inside most induction hobs, the IGBT, was conceived by an engineer born in India, B. Jayant Baliga.
